evidence.claim: Sandhills Journey follows Nebraska Highway 2 for 272 miles between Alliance and Grand Island.
evidence.quote: Sandhills Journey Scenic Byway (awarded National Scenic Byway) 272 miles on Nebraska Highway 2 from Grand Island to Alliance.

evidence.claim: The Nebraska Department of Transportation lists it among the state’s scenic byways and records its National Scenic Byway designation.
evidence.quote: Sandhills Journey Scenic Byway (awarded National Scenic Byway)

evidence.claim: East of Alliance, the highway enters the Sandhills, a region of mixed-grass prairie on dunes held in place by vegetation.
evidence.quote: At Alliance, N-2 goes east into the Sand Hills.

evidence.claim: Shallow lakes occupy low valleys between dunes, and most of the region has never been plowed.
evidence.quote: temporary and permanent shallow lakes are common in low-lying valleys between the grass-stabilized dunes

evidence.claim: The towns along this corridor took shape with the railroad.
evidence.quote: Thedford was established in 1887 when the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad was extended to that point

evidence.claim: The Chicago, Burlington and Quincy reached Thedford in 1887 and selected Ellsworth for a depot and water stop in 1888.
evidence.quote: In 1888 the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad chose the site as a location for a depot and water stop on their newly built line.

evidence.claim: That same year, Bartlett Richards began assembling the Spade Ranch, making Ellsworth its company town.
evidence.quote: Cattleman Bartlett Richards began assembling the expansive Spade Ranch in the same year, making Ellsworth a company town for the ranch.

evidence.claim: Cattle shipping joined the settlement to the railway.
evidence.quote: a shipping point for cattle on the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad.

evidence.quote: Thedford was established in 1887 when the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad was extended to that point

evidence.claim: Drive east from Alliance through Hyannis and Mullen to Thedford.
evidence.quote: At Alliance, N-2 goes east into the Sand Hills.  It goes through several small towns, including Hyannis, Mullen and Thedford.

evidence.claim: Near Halsey, the Nebraska National Forest interrupts the journey through grassland.
evidence.quote: East of Thedford, near Halsey, is the Nebraska National Forest.

evidence.claim: At Dunning, Highway 2 turns southeast toward Broken Bow.
evidence.quote: At Dunning, N-2 intersects N-91 and turns southeasterly towards Broken Bow and Grand Island.

evidence.claim: Continue through Ravenna and Cairo to Grand Island, where the road widens to four divided lanes on the city’s northwest edge.
evidence.quote: N-2 meets N-10 in Hazard, N-68 in Ravenna and N-11 in Cairo.  On the northwest edge of Grand Island, N-2 becomes a four-lane divided highway

evidence.claim: Ellsworth linked a cattle ranch to a railroad: the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy chose it for a depot and water stop in 1888.
evidence.quote: In 1888 the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad chose the site as a location for a depot and water stop on their newly built line.

evidence.claim: Bartlett Richards began assembling the Spade Ranch that year and made Ellsworth its company town.
evidence.quote: Cattleman Bartlett Richards began assembling the expansive Spade Ranch in the same year, making Ellsworth a company town for the ranch.

evidence.claim: Cattle shipped out by rail, while freight wagons carried supplies north to ranch headquarters.
evidence.quote: a shipping point for cattle on the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad.

evidence.claim: A two-story store built in 1898 supplied those wagons.
evidence.quote: In 1898, the two-story Spade Ranch Store was built; it supplied freight wagons going north to the Spade Ranch Headquarters.

evidence.claim: The Old Spade Ranch Store remains the village’s only operating business.
evidence.quote: The Old Spade Ranch Store is the only business currently operating in the village.

evidence.claim: The Bessey District began as a test of whether forest could be established on treeless Great Plains land.
evidence.quote: as an experiment to see if forests could be recreated in treeless areas of the Great Plains for use as a national timber reserve.

evidence.claim: In 1902, botanist Charles Edwin Bessey and Gifford Pinchot persuaded President Theodore Roosevelt to set aside two treeless tracts of Nebraska sandhills as forest reserves.
evidence.quote: University of Nebraska botany professor Charles Edwin Bessey, with the assistance of Gifford Pinchot, first Forest Service Chief, convinced President Theodore Roosevelt to set aside two treeless tracts of Nebraska sandhills as "forest reserves."

evidence.claim: Bessey wanted to grow timber against a feared national shortage caused by fires, unregulated cutting and rising demand for wood.
evidence.quote: Bessey's intent was to grow trees, which would offset what some thought would be a national timber shortage from large fires, unregulated harvest, and the country's growing appetite for wood products.

evidence.claim: The experiment produced a 20,000-acre planted forest within the larger ranger district.
evidence.quote: This effort resulted in a 20,000-acre (31.3 sq mi; 80.9 km2) forest

evidence.claim: Its Bessey Tree Nursery is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
evidence.quote: The Bessey Tree Nursery is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
The Nebraska National Forests & Grasslands began in 1902 as an experiment.

evidence.claim: Broken Bow’s name reached the U.S. Post Office Department through homesteader Wilson Hewitt.
evidence.quote: was submitted by homesteader Wilson Hewitt to the U.S. Post Office Department.

evidence.claim: It likely came from a settler’s discovery of a broken bow in a field at a former Native American camping ground.
evidence.quote: Its name, likely suggested by a settler who found a broken bow in a field at the site of a former Native American camping ground

evidence.claim: The town was platted in 1882, before the railroad arrived in 1884.
evidence.quote: Broken Bow was platted in 1882.

evidence.claim: That year it incorporated as a village; city status followed in 1888.
evidence.quote: The railroad was built through Broken Bow in 1884, and the town was incorporated as a village that same year. Broken Bow was incorporated as a city of the second class in 1888.

evidence.claim: Broken Bow is the seat of Custer County.
evidence.quote: It is the county seat of Custer County.

evidence.claim: The region sits over the Ogallala Aquifer, whose water reaches the surface in ponds and lakes between the grass-covered dunes.
evidence.quote: The Sandhills' thousands of ponds and lakes are spring-fed surface water areas of the Ogallala Aquifer.

evidence.claim: Hyannis was also laid out in 1888 as the railroad reached it.
evidence.quote: Hyannis was laid out in 1888 when the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad was extended to that point.

evidence.claim: The town’s schoolhouse came later, in 1932, and served Ellsworth until 2007, adding a longer civic history to the ranch depot.
evidence.quote: The Ellsworth School House, built in 1932, served Ellsworth until 2007.

evidence.claim: The ranger district has an office in Halsey.
evidence.quote: There is a local ranger district office in Halsey.

flags: The official cache confirms length and National Scenic Byway status but supplies no route-specific designation rationale, date, campaign or highway construction history. Railroad history is explicitly corridor context. Drive time is not sourced.

Dropped the current spring crane claim: cached evidence supports migratory cranes and stopover waters, but not that seasonal detail. Other current claims are supported; the forest superlative and dune height were omitted for focus.

The forest’s 1902 experiment is distinct from the 1907 consolidation establishing Nebraska National Forest. Planted acreage is described as the experiment’s result, not a verified present inventory; no current manager page is cached.
Broken Bow’s name origin remains qualified as likely, as in the source. No named Native nation is supplied for the former camping ground.
Broken Bow is shorter than 90 words because its supported name-and-railroad story is simple; unrelated census, business and celebrity facts were not added to fill space.
